All 3 laws

A planet's orbit about the Sun is an ellipse. The Sun's center is always located at one focus of the orbital ellipse.

A planet moves in its ellipse so that the line between it and the Sun placed at a focus sweeps out equal areas in equal

The square of the time period of the planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis of its orbit.

T2∝a3T^2 \propto a^3

A planet's orbit about the Sun is an ellipse. The Sun's center is always located at one focus of the orbital ellipse.

  • Apogee and perigee
  • Aphelion and perihelion
  • Apsis and periapsis

Kepler’s third law(Law of period)

The square of the time period of the planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis of its orbit.

T2∝a3T^2 \propto a^3
T=2πa3GMT = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a^3}{GM}}
T=2πr3GMT = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}} for circular orbit
Note: →r=R+h\rightarrow r = R + h

Shell theorem

Gravitational force inside a shell due to shell is zero

Question
What is the direction of force on m1m_1
Solution
a hemisphere is not a shell — the half that would have cancelled is missing, so what is left pulls the mass toward the missing cap, straight up the axis of symmetry
Question
What is net gravitational force on centre mass m
Solution
the shell contributes nothing at its own centre, so only the outside mass at distance dd is left
F=Gm2d2F = \frac{G m^2}{d^2}

Rediscover Newton law from Kepler's law Not Required

From Kepler 2nd Law

This can only be possible if Angular momentum is constant
This can only be possible if force is towards the centre so that torque is zero

From Kepler 3rd Law ⇒T2∝r3\Rightarrow T^2 \propto r^3

⇒Gm1m2rn=mv2r\Rightarrow G m_1 m_2 r^n = \frac{mv^2}{r}
=mω2r= m\omega^2 r
=m[2πT]2r= m\left[\frac{2\pi}{T}\right]^2 r
⇒T2=r1−n\Rightarrow T^2 = r^{1-n}
⇒1−n=3\Rightarrow 1 - n = 3
⇒n=−2\Rightarrow n = -2

Labeling the distance of closest approach r1r_1, and the speed at that point v1v_1, the furthest point r2r_2, the speed there v2v_2, we have

mv1r1=mv2r2=Lm v_1 r_1 = m v_2 r_2 = L

and

12mv12−GMm/r1=12mv22−GMm/r2=E.\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2 - GMm/r_1 = \frac{1}{2} m v_2^2 - GMm/r_2 = E.

From the second equation,

12mv12−GMm/r1−(12mv22−GMm/r2)=0.\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2 - GMm/r_1 - \left(\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2 - GMm/r_2\right) = 0.

Rearranging, and dropping the common factor mm,

12(v12−v22)=GM(1r1−1r2).\frac{1}{2}\left(v_1^2 - v_2^2\right) = GM\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right).

Using the angular momentum equation to write v1=L/mr1,v2=L/mr2v_1 = L/mr_1, v_2 = L/mr_2 and substituting these values in this equation gives L2L^2 in terms of r1,r2r_1, r_2 :

L22m2(1r12−1r22)=L22m2(1r1+1r2)(1r1−1r2)=GM(1r1−1r2)\frac{L^2}{2m^2}\left(\frac{1}{r_1^2} - \frac{1}{r_2^2}\right) = \frac{L^2}{2m^2}\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right) = GM\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right)

from which

L22m2=GM(1r1+1r2).\frac{L^2}{2m^2} = \frac{GM}{\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right)}.

The area of the ellipse is πab\pi ab (recall it's a circle squashed by a factor b/ab/a in one direction, so πa2\pi a^2 becomes πab\pi ab ), and the rate of sweeping out of area is L/2mL/2m, so the time TT for a complete orbit is given by:

T2=(πab)2L2/4m2=2(πab)2GM(1r1+1r2)T^2 = \frac{(\pi ab)^2}{L^2/4m^2} = \frac{2(\pi ab)^2}{GM}\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right)

Therefore

r1r2=b2r_1 r_2 = b^2

Also from the figure

r1+r22=a\frac{r_1 + r_2}{2} = a

so we have the amusing result that

the semimajor axis aa is the arithmetic mean of r1,r2r_1, r_2 and the semi-minor axis bb is their geometric mean, and furthermore

(1r1+1r2)=r1+r2r1r2=2ab2.\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right) = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{r_1 r_2} = \frac{2a}{b^2}.

Deriving Kepler's Law

We can immediately use the above result to express the angular momentum LL very simply:

L22m2=GM(1r1+1r2)=GMb22a.\frac{L^2}{2m^2} = \frac{GM}{\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right)} = \frac{GMb^2}{2a}.

We're now ready to find the time for one orbit TT. Remember TT is the total area of the orbit divided by the rate area is swept out, and that rate is L/2mL/2m, so:

T2=(πab)2L2/4m2=2(πab)22aGMb2=4π2a3GM.T^2 = \frac{(\pi ab)^2}{L^2/4m^2} = \frac{2(\pi ab)^2 2a}{GMb^2} = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{GM}.

That is,

T2=4π2a3GMT^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{GM}

A simple generalization of the result for circular orbits.

To prove that the total energy only depends on the length of the major axis, we simply add the total energies at the two extreme points:

12mv12−GMmr1+12mv22−GMm/r2=2E.\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2 - \frac{GMm}{r_1} + \frac{1}{2} m v_2^2 - GMm/r_2 = 2E.

The substitution v1=L/mr1,v2=L/mr2v_1 = L/mr_1, v_2 = L/mr_2 in this equation gives

L22m(1r12+1r22)−GMm(1r1+1r2)=2E.\frac{L^2}{2m}\left(\frac{1}{r_1^2} + \frac{1}{r_2{}^2}\right) - GMm\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right) = 2E.

Writing

(1r12+1r22)=(1r1+1r2)2−2r1r2,\left(\frac{1}{r_1^2} + \frac{1}{r_2^2}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right)^2 - \frac{2}{r_1 r_2},

it is easy to check that

E=−GMr1+r2=−GM2aE = -\frac{GM}{r_1 + r_2} = -\frac{GM}{2a}

Writing

(1r12+1r22)=(1r1+1r2)2−2r1r2,\left(\frac{1}{r_1^2} + \frac{1}{r_2^2}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right)^2 - \frac{2}{r_1 r_2},

it is easy to check that

E=−GMr1+r2=−GM2aE = -\frac{GM}{r_1 + r_2} = -\frac{GM}{2a}
